metadata.title: Night Yard: Inside the Godot Code
metadata.audience: makers following the channel's Claude + Walker game workflows
metadata.note: godot-gamedev walker film. Code panels are Godot editor reconstructions with verbatim source; each is followed by real engine output of the same build. No game change, no paid calls, no upload.

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. That's the kind of prompt Walker expects, reconstructed here, not a transcript. This time we open the project itself: a piece of code, then the exact thing it does on screen, in the real build.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a 2.5D brawler-platformer — a night shift in a container yard, three Y Bots to choose from, ledges, wall jumps, an axe and a hammer, and a Forewoman at the end — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: Art from the Unity folder; levels and sound authored.

beats.narration_text: Night Yard is built in code. Its six level scenes are seven lines each, and fifty-two hundred lines of GDScript build every block, bot and menu at runtime, from text maps. So every piece of code we read has a result you can watch.

props.text:
Night Yard
is built from scenes.
Six level scenes, seven lines each,
and 5,215 lines of GDScript
that build every level.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: Open a level scene and there's one node. Run it for eight seconds, and level dot g d has built the rest: an environment and a moonlight, blocks and containers, the yard pack behind the lane, the spike trap, the fighters, the HUD and the camera. Three hundred and eighty-five nodes.

beats.narration_text: Attack on the ground means whatever fits first. If you're holding the axe, swing or throw it. If you're on a weapon, pick it up. Behind an unaware bot, a takedown. Down means the hammer, if it's charged. And up means an uppercut, or a dragon punch when running.

beats.narration_text: In play: jab, cross, up and attack for the uppercut, K to block, then down and attack, and the hammer comes down.

beats.narration_text: Every attack checks for hits only inside its hit window, measured from the clip. A throw lets go of the axe at its release time. And if you press attack again after the hit starts, the next part of the combo is queued and plays at its own moment.

props.title: A Combo Is a Window
props.code:
# Hit window
	var hit: Array = a["hit"]
	if t >= hit[0] and t <= hit[1]:
		_check_hits()
	# WeaponThrow at ThrowTiming
	if attack_id == "throw" and not _released_axe and t >= a["release"]:
		_released_axe = true
		throw_weapon()
	# Combos: attack again inside the window chains the next part (TransitionIndexer + ATTACK)
	if a.has("combo") and _attack_buffer > 0.0 and t >= hit[0]:
		_queued_attack = a["combo"]
		_attack_buffer = 0.0
	if _queued_attack != "" and t >= a["combo_at"]:
		_start_attack(_queued_attack)

notes.value: damage only inside the hit window

notes.label: Chain
notes.value: attack again → the next part at combo_at

beats.narration_text: Throwing is short. The fighter lets go of the weapon, the throw is counted for the playtest, and the axe is launched from shoulder height in the direction the fighter faces.

props.title: Throwing the Axe
props.code:
func throw_weapon() -> void:
	if holding == null:
		return
	var w := holding
	holding = null
	stats["throws"] += 1
	w.throw(self, global_position + Vector3(facing * 0.6, 1.25, 0), facing)

beats.narration_text: A bot notices you if you're in front of it, within eight metres. Behind its back, only if you're right next to it, or running close by. Fighting nearby is noise, and that wakes it too.

beats.narration_text: And this is the takedown test: a bot just ahead of you, facing the same way, so you're behind it, that has not noticed you, standing or walking on the same floor. The boss is never a target.

props.title: The Takedown Test
props.code:
func _takedown_victim() -> Fighter:
	for other in get_tree().get_nodes_in_group("fighters"):
		var f: Fighter = other
		if f == self or f.team == team or f.state == S.DEAD or f.kind == "sophie":
			continue
		var d := f.global_position - global_position
		# behind an enemy that has not noticed you, both on the same floor
		if d.x * facing > 0.2 and d.x * facing < 1.3 and absf(d.y) < 0.3 and f.facing == facing \
				and not f.aware and f.is_on_floor() and f.state in [S.IDLE, S.WALK]:
			return f
	return null

notes.value: behind, 0.2–1.3 m, same floor

notes.label: Who
notes.value: unaware, idle or walking, not the boss

beats.narration_text: A spike plate is a small state machine. Ready, until a fighter stands on it. Then armed, and after the delay it fires. Anyone still on the plate is killed by the spikes. Then it reloads.

beats.narration_text: The rest of the project, in one pass. A main menu, a character-select stage, a How to play page, and credits. An audio autoload with synthesized sounds and music. A kit autoload for the characters and props. Tools that convert and retarget the Unity art, and a playtest that wires the bot brain into the player. The film's captures pressed the keys instead.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This is a project you can read top to bottom: thin scenes, levels as text, one fighter class for everyone. Two real defects live in the menus: an options panel that keeps the pause key, and arrow keys that also move the focus. The game's own test never opened a menu, so it never saw them. And nobody has played it yet.

artifactLines: Implemented: 10 thin scenes; level.gd builds each level from an ASCII map.
Good habits: one fighter class, attacks measured from the clips, a grid-checked ledge.
Defects: options_panel.gd:53 keeps the pause key; arrows move the focus too.
Not judged: fun, difficulty, boss fairness. 0 human playtests.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude in your own Godot project: Use Walker on my Godot project. Find one key that two parts of my UI both listen to. Predict what happens when it's pressed. Then write a capture that presses it with real input and checks the result, and only after that, propose the smallest fix. Liam, in for Bear.
